response.text:
In the fog-bound heart of London, the interminable Chancery suit of Jarndyce and Jarndyce drags on, ruining lives across generations, while in fashionable society Lady Dedlock, wife of the proud baronet Sir Leicester, conceals a secret past that the family lawyer Tulkinghorn has begun to suspect. Esther Summerson, raised in joyless seclusion by a stern godmother who tells her she is her mother's disgrace, is taken under the guardianship of the kindly John Jarndyce and brought to Bleak House, where she becomes companion to two other wards of the suit, the radiant Ada Clare and the sanguine Richard Carstone. As Esther blossoms into the household's beloved "Dame Durden," Richard and Ada fall in love, and Richard, restless and unable to settle to any profession, begins to stake his hopes on the Chancery suit, falling under the bloodless sway of the lawyer Vholes. A chance meeting between Esther and Lady Dedlock in Lincolnshire stirs an inexplicable recognition, and through Tulkinghorn's patient detective work and the clues left by a dead law-writer named Nemo — who proves to have been Lady Dedlock's long-lost lover and Esther's father — the secret of Esther's true parentage moves slowly toward exposure.

Esther catches smallpox while nursing the destitute crossing-sweeper Jo, and her face is permanently scarred; recovering at Mr. Boythorn's, she is at last embraced by her mother, who confesses everything before insisting they must remain forever apart. Tulkinghorn, having pieced the story together, torments Lady Dedlock with the threat of disclosure until he is found shot dead in his chambers, and suspicion falls first on the honest old trooper George Rouncewell — who proves to be the long-estranged son of the Dedlock housekeeper — before Inspector Bucket, with patient cunning, exposes the real murderess as Lady Dedlock's vindictive French maid Hortense.

When Sir Leicester learns the truth he forgives his wife unreservedly, but she has already fled in shame; Bucket and Esther pursue her through a freezing night across the country and back to London, only to find her dead at the gate of the squalid burying-ground where her lover lies. His own designs gently set aside, Mr. Jarndyce — who had proposed marriage to Esther out of protective love — quietly arranges instead her union with the steadfast young surgeon Allan Woodcourt, presenting the couple with a second Bleak House in Yorkshire as a wedding gift. The Jarndyce suit is finally called in court only to collapse when it is discovered that the entire estate has been consumed in legal costs, and Richard, broken by the news, dies in Ada's arms, leaving her with a son to raise under Jarndyce's care. Around these central griefs, a great gallery of figures plays out the novel's themes of neglect, philanthropy, and entangled responsibility — the telescopic philanthropist Mrs. Jellyby, the airy parasite Skimpole, the deportment-mongering Turveydrops, the Smallweeds, the law-stationer Snagsby, the rag-and-bottle man Krook who dies by spontaneous combustion, the ever-hopeful madwoman Miss Flite with her caged birds, and poor Jo, hounded to death by the very system that ignores him. Settled at last in her new home with husband and children, with Ada and little Richard often beside them and her guardian as constant friend, Esther closes her narrative in quiet gratitude, suggesting that whatever beauty she has lost has been more than repaid by the love that has surrounded her — and that the great fog of Chancery, having devoured one family's fortune, rolls on unchanged over a country that allows it to.
